chapter.title: Machine Vision
chapter.prerequisites: Chapter 2, especially 2.8 Vision-Guided Picking, and Chapter 3 for Lesson 7.6.
chapter.handsOn: process camera images with OpenCV, configure point cloud filters, and build a ROS 2 camera pipeline in Python.
chapter.summary: Industrial camera sensors and optics, machine vision lighting techniques, 2D image processing, 3D point cloud perception, automated inspection, and a ROS 2 camera pipeline.

lessons.title: Industrial Cameras and Optics
objectives: Compare CMOS and CCD image sensor architectures, evaluating readout speed, blooming resistance, and pixel saturation capacity.
Distinguish global shutter from rolling shutter mechanisms, explaining how exposure timing affects moving parts and how strobe lighting prevents rolling shutter distortion.
Calculate lens aperture stops and optical throughput using f-numbers, and analyze the trade-off between depth of field and light throughput.
Explain how telecentric lenses eliminate parallax error in precision dimensional gauging and describe how the GenICam standard provides hardware-independent camera control.

lessons.title: Lighting for Machine Vision
objectives: Select appropriate illumination geometries—including backlighting, ring lighting, glancing, and darkfield—based on part geometry, surface finish, and inspection goals.
Explain how diffuse dome lights and coaxial beamsplitters reduce glare and hot spots on curved and flat shiny surfaces.
Use colored filters matched to the light, infrared cut-off filters and cross-polarization to bring out target features and reject ambient factory light.
Evaluate the benefits of pulsed strobe illumination and LED overdriving for freezing rapid part motion and extending emitter life expectancy.

lessons.title: Image Processing Basics
objectives: Convert raw camera frames across color spaces (BGR, Grayscale, HSV) and isolate chromatic targets using color segmentation masks.
Analyze intensity distributions with grayscale histograms and apply global, Otsu, and adaptive thresholding to segment foreground objects.
Extract object contours, calculate centroid coordinates from spatial image moments, and filter connected components by area.
Detect and characterize circular objects using SimpleBlobDetector, trace boundaries with Canny edge detection, and locate parts with template matching.

lessons.title: 3D Sensing
objectives: Differentiate direct physical 3D sensing (LiDAR, structured light, stereo) from neural network 2D depth inference.
Calculate physical depth from stereo camera disparity, baseline distance, and focal length using triangulation geometry.
Filter and downsample raw point clouds using PCL PassThrough, VoxelGrid, and StatisticalOutlierRemoval algorithms.
Segment planar supporting surfaces with RANSAC and extract individual workpiece clusters using Euclidean cluster extraction.

lessons.title: Inspection and Measurement
objectives: Explain the two kinds of inspection error, missed defects and false alarms, and what each costs a production line.
Apply spatial resolution metrics and the Nyquist sampling limit to determine the optical tolerance limits of a camera sensor.
Explain how optical distortion is classified into barrel and pincushion types and corrected through camera calibration.
Name the ISO/IEC 15416 and 15415 print quality standards for 1D and 2D codes, and explain how Reed-Solomon error correction lets a damaged Data Matrix ECC 200 symbol still be read.

lessons.title: Lab: A ROS 2 Camera Pipeline
objectives: Describe the ROS 2 camera pipeline architecture and message definitions (sensor_msgs/Image and sensor_msgs/CameraInfo).
Interpret optical camera coordinate frame conventions (+x right, +y down, +z forward) and map them to robot base frames.
Manage network bandwidth using image_transport plugins and synchronize image and calibration streams with message_filters TimeSynchronizer.
Implement a complete ROS 2 Python node using cv_bridge to convert images between ROS messages and OpenCV NumPy arrays for real-time edge processing.

blurbs.7-1: Industrial camera sensors and optics: CMOS versus CCD, global and rolling shutters, pixel size and Nyquist resolution, focal length and f-number, telecentric lenses, and GenICam.
blurbs.7-2: Illumination for machine vision: backlighting, ring, glancing, darkfield, diffuse dome, coaxial and in-line lighting, optical filters, cross-polarization, and LED strobing.
blurbs.7-3: Core 2D image processing: color space conversion, histograms and contrast equalization, global, Otsu and adaptive thresholding, contours, moments, blobs, Canny edge detection, and template matching.
blurbs.7-4: 3D perception for robotics: direct sensing versus 2D inference, stereo disparity geometry, point cloud filtering with PCL (PassThrough, VoxelGrid, outliers), RANSAC planes, Euclidean clustering, and bin picking.
blurbs.7-5: Automated inspection and measurement: optical resolution and the Nyquist limit, telecentric gauging, lens distortion calibration, presence verification, and 1D/2D barcode quality.
blurbs.7-6: Build a ROS 2 camera pipeline in Python: sensor_msgs/Image and CameraInfo, optical frames, image_transport, cv_bridge conversion, and real-time OpenCV edge processing; runs without a camera using cam2image test images.

glossary.adaptive thresholding: A binarization technique that calculates distinct local thresholds for small image regions to handle uneven lighting gradients across a scene.
glossary.backlighting: An illumination technique placing the light source behind the object to create a high-contrast opaque silhouette for boundary and dimensional inspection.
glossary.barrel distortion: An optical lens aberration where magnification decreases toward the periphery, causing straight rectangular lines to bow outward like a barrel.
glossary.Canny edge detector: A multi-stage edge detection algorithm that uses Gaussian smoothing, intensity gradients, non-maximum suppression, and hysteresis thresholding to find thin, robust boundaries.
glossary.CMOS sensor: A solid-state image sensor where each pixel has its own amplifier and readout circuitry, enabling fast frame rates and low power consumption.
glossary.coaxial illumination: A lighting geometry using a beamsplitter to project diffuse light along the camera's optical axis, reducing shadows and glare on flat specular surfaces.
glossary.cross-polarization: A technique using a polarizer on the light source and an analyzer on the camera lens oriented at 90 degrees to eliminate direct specular glare from reflective surfaces.
glossary.cv_bridge: A ROS package providing bidirectional conversion functions between ROS Image messages and OpenCV NumPy array buffers.
glossary.darkfield illumination: A shallow-angle lighting technique where direct rays reflect away from the lens and surface flaws or scratches scatter light into the camera as bright features.
glossary.Data Matrix ECC 200: A two-dimensional matrix barcode symbology that uses an L-shaped finder pattern and Reed-Solomon error correction to reconstruct damaged codes.
glossary.diffuse dome light: A hemispherical light fixture that reflects omnidirectional scattered light downward to evenly illuminate curved reflective objects without hot spots or harsh shadows.
glossary.dimensional gauging: The precise physical measurement of part dimensions—such as lengths, diameters, and clearances—from calibrated camera image coordinates.
glossary.disparity: The horizontal pixel displacement between corresponding object points in the left and right images of a calibrated stereo camera pair, inversely proportional to depth.
glossary.Euclidean cluster extraction: A 3D point cloud segmentation algorithm that groups neighboring points into distinct object clusters based on spatial proximity thresholds.
glossary.f-number: The ratio of a lens's focal length to its effective aperture diameter, governing light throughput and depth of field.
glossary.GenICam: A vendor-neutral software standard from EMVA that provides a universal programming interface and feature naming convention for industrial machine vision cameras.
glossary.global shutter: An electronic shutter mechanism that starts and stops exposure simultaneously across all sensor pixels, preventing motion distortion.
glossary.histogram equalization: An image processing method that redistributes pixel intensity levels across the entire dynamic range to improve image contrast.
glossary.HSV color space: A color representation separating image data into hue (color type), saturation (color purity), and value (brightness) channels.
glossary.image moments: Weighted average calculations of image pixel intensities used to determine geometric properties such as area, orientation, and centroid coordinates.
glossary.image_transport: A ROS 2 package suite providing transparent runtime plugin support for publishing and subscribing to compressed image streams.
glossary.Nyquist limit: The theoretical maximum spatial frequency an image sensor can resolve without aliasing, requiring at least two detector pixels per line pair.
glossary.Otsu binarization: An automatic thresholding method that determines an optimal global cutoff by minimizing intra-class intensity variance on bimodal histograms.
glossary.PassThrough filter: A PCL filtering method that removes 3D point cloud data falling outside user-specified minimum and maximum coordinate bounds along a selected axis.
glossary.pincushion distortion: An optical lens aberration where magnification increases toward the periphery, pulling straight lines outward from the center.
glossary.plumb_bob: The standard radial and tangential camera lens distortion model in ROS 2, parameterized by five polynomial coefficients (k1, k2, t1, t2, k3).
glossary.point cloud: A set of data points in 3D Cartesian coordinates representing physical external surfaces sampled by depth sensors.
glossary.presence verification: An automated inspection check that confirms whether required components, fasteners, or features are present before a part advances.
glossary.RANSAC: Random Sample Consensus; an iterative mathematical algorithm that estimates model parameters from data containing a high proportion of outliers, commonly used to detect geometric planes.
glossary.rolling shutter: An electronic shutter mechanism that exposes pixel rows sequentially with a temporal offset, which can distort fast-moving objects.
glossary.sensor_msgs/CameraInfo: The standard ROS 2 message structure carrying intrinsic camera parameters, distortion coefficients, and rectification matrices.
glossary.sensor_msgs/Image: The standard ROS 2 message structure for transmitting uncompressed raster image pixel matrices with row step and encoding metadata.
glossary.StatisticalOutlierRemoval: A PCL denoising filter that computes mean neighbor distances and discards isolated points whose distance exceeds a statistical standard deviation threshold.
glossary.strobe mode: Pulsing an LED light source with brief microsecond bursts synchronized to camera exposure, reducing heat and allowing high-current overdriving to freeze fast motion.
glossary.telecentric lens: A specialized optical lens with chief rays parallel to the optical axis, eliminating parallax error and maintaining constant magnification across varying object distances.
glossary.template matching: A computer vision technique that slides a small reference template image across a larger search image to find the position of highest visual correlation.
glossary.TimeSynchronizer: A message_filters synchronization utility that aligns multiple incoming ROS 2 topic streams by matching their header timestamps.
glossary.VoxelGrid filter: A PCL downsampling algorithm that partitions 3D space into regular cubic voxels and replaces all points within each voxel with their centroid.

quiz.question: Why are global shutter cameras preferred over rolling shutter cameras when imaging moving parts on a conveyor?
choices: Global shutters have significantly lower ambient noise in dark scenes
All sensor pixels start and stop exposing simultaneously, preventing geometric rolling shutter distortion
Global shutters do not require an imaging lens
Global shutters double the depth of field of the lens
quiz.explanation: During image acquisition with a global shutter, all sensor pixels start and stop exposing at the same time, preventing the geometric image distortion caused by relative motion during rolling shutter acquisition.

quiz.question: What happens to a lens aperture and its light throughput when its f-number is increased by a factor of the square root of two?
choices: The aperture area is halved and light throughput decreases by a factor of two
The aperture area doubles and throughput increases by two
The focal length increases by 50% while throughput stays constant
The depth of field drops to zero
quiz.explanation: Increasing the f-number by a factor of the square root of two halves the aperture area and reduces lens light throughput by a factor of two.

quiz.question: Which illumination technique is best suited for inspecting scratches, cracks, and bubbles in clear or translucent materials?
quiz.explanation: Darkfield illumination introduces light at shallow angles so light scatters off surface flaws, producing high contrast by highlighting scratches, cracks, and bubbles in clear materials.

quiz.question: How does cross-polarization reject unwanted glare from shiny reflective surfaces?
choices: By flashing an LED strobe at five times its continuous current
By shifting the optical wavelength into the near-infrared spectrum
By using an object-space telecentric lens with an internal beamsplitter
By placing a polarizer on the light source and an analyzer on the lens oriented at 90 degrees
quiz.explanation: Cross-polarization uses a polarizer on the illumination source and an analyzer on the camera lens oriented at 90 degrees to achieve maximum rejection of unwanted glare.

quiz.question: In OpenCV HSV color space representation, what numerical ranges are assigned to the hue, saturation, and value channels?
choices: Hue 0 to 255, Saturation 0 to 255, Value 0 to 255
Hue 0 to 179, Saturation 0 to 255, Value 0 to 255
Hue 0 to 360, Saturation 0 to 100, Value 0 to 100
Hue 0 to 180, Saturation 0 to 180, Value 0 to 180
quiz.explanation: In OpenCV HSV color space, the hue channel spans from 0 to 179 while saturation and value span from 0 to 255.

quiz.question: What dimensions are produced for the output correlation matrix when matching a template of size w × h across an image of size W × H?
quiz.explanation: In template matching, comparing an image of size W × H with a template of size w × h produces an output match matrix of size (W - w + 1, H - h + 1).

quiz.question: In stereo vision triangulation, what is the mathematical relationship between depth Z, physical baseline B, lens focal length f, and disparity?
quiz.explanation: In stereo vision triangulation, depth Z is inversely proportional to disparity according to the relationship disparity = (baseline * f) / depth, which yields depth = (baseline * f) / disparity.

quiz.question: How does the PCL VoxelGrid filter downsample dense point clouds?
choices: By deleting every alternating point along the sensor scan lines
By fitting a RANSAC plane to the scene and discarding all inliers
By measuring neighbor distances and removing points exceeding two standard deviations
By partitioning 3D space into voxel boxes and replacing all points inside each box with their centroid
quiz.explanation: The PCL VoxelGrid filter downsamples point clouds by partitioning 3D space into voxel boxes and replacing all points inside each box with their centroid.

quiz.question: Under the Nyquist limit, what is the minimum sensor sampling requirement to resolve an optical line pair?
choices: At least two pixels per line pair
quiz.explanation: The Nyquist limit represents the highest spatial frequency a sensor can sample and requires at least two pixels per line pair (one pixel on the bright bar and one on the dark bar).

quiz.question: Which version of Data Matrix barcode uses Reed-Solomon error correction to detect damage and reconstruct corrupted codewords?
quiz.explanation: Data Matrix ECC 200 is the only Data Matrix version that utilizes Reed-Solomon error correction to detect damage locations and reconstruct corrupted codewords.

quiz.question: In the standard ROS optical camera coordinate frame convention, in which directions do the coordinate axes point?
choices: +x right, +y down, +z into the image plane
+x left, +y up, +z into the image plane
quiz.explanation: In the ROS optical camera coordinate frame, +x points right, +y points down, and +z points into the image plane along the optical axis.

quiz.question: In cv_bridge, which function converts an incoming ROS sensor_msgs/Image message into an OpenCV NumPy array?
quiz.explanation: In cv_bridge, imgmsg_to_cv2 converts a ROS Image message into an OpenCV NumPy image with an optional desired_encoding format.
